subject: Textiles
intro: Three complete textiles lessons: compare materials and joins, design for a user, then construct and evaluate a prototype. Weeks 5–6 adapt the uploaded shared BUILD/GROW lessons; Week 7 is newly authored completion from the GROW scheme-of-work sequence. The GROW route adds repeated-test reasoning, dimensioned plans and evidence-based improvements.

sources.title: Original classroom pattern and sample data
sources.note: All designs, exact dimensions, fictional users and sample join/prototype records were authored for this pack. Data are illustrative, not test certificates. Actual material, adhesive, tool and handling/cure instructions require school approval. No formal ASDAN/AQA attainment or award is promised.

lessons.title: Test materials and joins
lessons.big_question: Which material and join fit the job?
lessons.objective: Compare fabric properties and joining methods using observations and a fair-test record.
success: I can link a fabric property to something I observe.
I can compare glue, tape and stitch evidence without assuming a winner.
I can explain one suitable choice and one limit of the test.

vocabulary.meaning: A feature of a material that can be observed or tested.
The area where one piece lies on another.
A comparison that keeps relevant conditions consistent.

slides.title: Test materials and joins
body: Today: inspect samples, try a cold join and read test evidence.
Choose handling, looking, reading or recording. You do not have to touch a fabric.
slides.prompt: How could we check a claim about a material?
slides.answer: Observe or test the actual sample and record what happens.
slides.notes: Adapts uploaded Week 5 PPTX, log and worksheet. Removes the assumed “thread wins” outcome, hidden feely-bag requirement and compulsory needle task.

slides.title: Property plus evidence
body: “Flexible” means it bends. “Stretchy” means its length changes under a gentle pull.
“This cut edge stays together” is an observation about this sample.
A material’s name does not prove every property.
slides.prompt: Does a fabric that bends have to stretch?
slides.answer: No. Bending and changing length are different properties.
slides.notes: Show known clean samples or use the full fictional specimen cards; do not infer fibre composition from appearance alone.

slides.title: Compare two samples
body: Inspect felt sample B and net sample E, or read their property cards.
Choose two property words for each.
Link a choice to the card-pocket job.
slides.prompt: Which sample is a better starting point for a card pocket, and why?
slides.answer: B: soft, flexible and opaque; its cut edge stayed together. The join still needs testing.
slides.notes: Accept alternatives supported by actual evidence. No forced tactile contact or personal sensory disclosure.

slides.title: Three ways to connect
body: Glue needs the amount and curing time on its label.
Cold fabric tape is pressed; we are not using iron-on tape.
A prepared stitch sample shows thread joining the layers.
slides.prompt: Can we test fresh glue as though it has already cured?
slides.answer: No. Use properly prepared samples or the labelled sample data.
slides.notes: Adults prepare stitched specimens before the lesson; no pupil needles, pins or heat are required.

slides.title: A fair comparison?
body: Team A tests fresh glue. Team B tests tape that is ready to handle.
Their strip sizes and overlaps are also different.
slides.prompt: Can they claim one method is stronger from this comparison?
slides.answer: No. Preparation, fabric dimensions and overlap differ; the test needs consistent conditions.
slides.notes: Use the full test-method resource. Do not conduct an uncontrolled pupil tug-of-war.

slides.title: Make, label, leave to cure
body: Join two prepared strips using approved cold tape, then make a glue sample if approved.
Label the method and record whether you made or only inspected it.
Leave wet glue to cure; inspect the adult’s prepared stitch sample.
slides.prompt: What should the record say if you observed the stitch sample?
slides.answer: “Inspected a stitched join”, not “made a stitch”.
slides.notes: Pupils can direct or use a paper model. Adult follows product instructions and supervises tool use; use supplied data for comparisons.

slides.title: Read the sample results
body: At the same 100 g load for 10 seconds: glue held 3/3, tape 1/3, stitch 2/3.
These are invented class results.
A holding test at one load does not find the maximum strength.
slides.prompt: What claim is supported?
slides.answer: Glue held most consistently in these three sample tests. It is not proof that glue is always strongest.
slides.notes: An adult may demonstrate the prepared test just above a tray if approved; no live weight testing is necessary.

slides.title: Match the join to the job
body: For a quick display repair, consider time and surface.
For a hem, consider fabric, movement and washing.
For a bag handle, further load and reinforcement checks are needed.
slides.prompt: Can this 100 g test certify a bag handle?
slides.answer: No. Its real load, repeated use, material and design need appropriate testing.
slides.notes: Collect reasoned choices, then return samples and tools and reset the workspace.

slides.title: One claim, one limit
body: Finish: “In this test ___ because ___.”
slides.prompt: Name one condition that should stay the same in the comparison.
slides.answer: Fabric, strip dimensions, overlap, load, time or handling.
slides.notes: Accept a pointed evidence card or short oral response; record real support given.

worksheet.title: Test materials and joins | Design and process record

tasks.heading: 1. Property evidence
tasks.prompt: Use sample B: soft, opaque, flexible, cut edge stayed together. Sample E: see-through holes, flexible.
items: Name two properties of B.
Name one property of E.
Which better suits a card pocket? Give a reason.
tasks.answer: B: any two supplied properties. E: see-through or flexible. B is a sensible starting choice because opaque/edge stays together; join suitability still needs checking.

tasks.heading: 2. Read repeated results
tasks.prompt: These are sample data. At the same load/time: glue held, held, held; tape opened, held, opened; stitch held, opened, held.
items: Count successful tests for each method.
Which gave the most consistent result here?
Does this prove that method is always strongest?
tasks.answer: Glue 3/3; tape 1/3; stitch 2/3. Glue most consistent here. No: actual materials, preparation and use can change the result.

tasks.heading: 3. Choose with a reason
tasks.prompt: Use the join cards and name further evidence where needed.
items: A temporary paper display needs a quick join.
A bag handle will carry items repeatedly.
Fresh glue has not had the label’s curing time.
tasks.answer: Approved cold tape may suit the display after a trial. Bag handle needs appropriate load/repetition/design tests. Leave glue to cure and use prepared specimens/sample data.

worksheet.exit_question: What is the difference between a made join and an inspected join?
worksheet.exit_answer: Made means the learner completed the process; inspected means they examined evidence of someone else’s join.

preparation: Print specimen, join and sample-data cards; provide known clean samples with accessible labels A–E.
Prepare 100 × 30 mm fabric strips and 20 × 30 mm overlaps; pre-cut where needed. Use only approved cold adhesives and check material sensitivities privately.
Prepare cured glue/tape specimens and a stitched display sample before the lesson, following actual product instructions. The default comparison uses supplied sample data.
materials: Known clean cotton/felt/denim/jersey/net samples or the complete property cards; paper/card alternative.
Adult-prepared strips, ruler, pencil/chalk, school-approved cold fabric glue and tape, labelled drying tray, adult-prepared stitched display.
If an adult demonstration is approved: sealed 100 g test load, tray and suitable prepared holding fixture; pupils do not handle the load.

timing.activity: Arrive, choose role and introduce the question.
Observe or read material properties.
Model three join methods and fair comparison.
Make/inspect joins and label a drying sample.
Interpret sample results and match a join to a job.
Count and return scissors, tools and sample pieces; close approved adhesive containers, collect tape backings and scraps, wipe the work surface as directed and wash hands if needed.
Individual evidence-and-limit exit.

teacher.modelling: Bend a specimen, then give an observation rather than a universal claim. Trace the prepared stitched join. Model the distinction between a fresh sample and one ready for testing, then count successes across all three sample repeats.
misconceptions: Bending is not the same as stretching.
Fabric name alone does not establish all properties.
A fresh adhesive sample cannot stand in for a correctly cured join.
The supplied data do not show that stitch always wins or that a real bag handle is safe.
teacher.support: Offer two named samples and one property contrast first. Read the cards aloud, accept pointing/drawing/scribing and allow a paper joining sample. Keep made/inspected/simulated records distinct.
teacher.stretch: Explain why repeats improve the evidence, identify one remaining limitation and design a safer fair comparison for an intended desk use without running an extra practical test.
teacher.fallback: Use the complete specimen descriptions and invented test record. Learners sequence preparation, curing, testing and recording, and inspect a drawing or written stitch description without tools.
teacher.safeguarding: Follow the school practical-work risk assessment and individual access plans. The default lessons use no needles, pins, irons, hot glue, cord loops or loose buttons/beads. Adults control, count and return scissors and any small test equipment; pre-cut pieces are available. Use only school-approved cold adhesives according to the actual product instructions, check skin/material sensitivities privately, and keep glue away from eyes and mouths. Touching fabric, wearing an item or accepting physical guidance is never required. Agree support; use demonstration, pointing, an observer role or a paper/card model. Keep personal identifiers and pupil photos off public website files.
teacher.assessment: Record a property with evidence, an accurate made/inspected distinction, a sample-result comparison and a reasoned join choice. Practical competence is recorded only for actions directly observed; no formal award is promised.

resources.title: Fabric property cards
resources.instructions: These are fictional specimen descriptions for an offline lesson. They describe these samples, not every fabric with the same name. Match a property to evidence; handle real samples only if you choose to.
items: A | Thin woven cotton sample: bends easily; its surface looks smooth; a freshly cut edge has loose threads. It barely stretches during this class’s gentle check.
B | Felt sample: feels soft; looks thicker than sample A; bends; its cut edge stays together in this class’s handling check. It barely stretches.
C | Denim sample: feels firmer and thicker than A; bends with more effort; its cut edge has loose threads. This sample has little stretch.
D | Knitted jersey sample: bends and stretches under a gentle pull, then moves back towards its starting shape. Its surface looks closely looped.
E | Net sample: visible holes let the card behind show through; it bends easily. A small loose item could pass through its holes.

Property word bank: flexible = bends; stretchy = changes length under a gentle pull; opaque = cannot see through; translucent/see-through = some light or details show through; thick/thin = relative thickness; frays = cut threads loosen.

Match jobs: a soft card pocket that keeps its cut edge together; a display overlay that reveals the card behind; a fabric item that needs stretch. Use the evidence on these cards, and name any further check needed.
answers: Pocket candidate: B, because this felt sample is soft, flexible and its edge stayed together. Its join still needs a suitable test.
See-through overlay: E. Its holes would be unsuitable for containing loose tiny items.
Stretch candidate: D. The amount of stretch and recovery must suit the real job.
A fabric name alone does not prove a property, suitability or join strength. Check the actual sample.

resources.title: Three join cards | What changes?
resources.instructions: Look at prepared samples or these written descriptions. The core practical makes glue and cold-tape samples; an adult-prepared stitched sample allows a third method to be inspected without pupil needle use.
items: GLUE: a school-approved cold fabric adhesive joins two overlapping fabric pieces. Use the amount and curing time on its label. A fresh wet sample is for drying, not immediate testing.

TAPE: cold, pressure-applied double-sided fabric tape joins an overlap when pressed as its label directs. Use a product approved for the actual material. Iron-on or heat-activated tape is not used in this pack.
STITCH: thread travels through both fabric layers to form a join. The display sample is prepared by an adult before the lesson; pupils may point to its thread path. No needle task is required.
Temporary paper display repair: speed may matter; approved cold tape can be considered after a quick trial on the actual surface.
Garment hem: consider the fabric, comfort, movement, washing and whether the join is temporary or lasting. The small classroom test cannot decide all of these.
Bag handle: it carries a load repeatedly. It needs an appropriate design, material, reinforcement and a test for its actual load; this lesson does not certify any handle as safe.
No method is always strongest, neatest or fastest for every material. A join can change when its overlap, adhesive, drying, stitches or test conditions change.
answers: A glue specimen must cure as directed before its performance can be judged.
Cold tape and iron-on tape are different products; the pack uses only the cold type.
Inspecting a stitched sample is valid learning, but must not be recorded as making a stitch.
Accept choices supported by the job and evidence; do not award a universal “thread wins” answer.

resources.title: Join test | Sample data and fair comparison
resources.instructions: These are invented class results, not tests carried out by the pupil or a guarantee about a product. All three methods were tested on the same type of felt and the same setup. Read the method before comparing.
items: SAMPLE SETUP: two felt strips, each 100 mm × 30 mm, overlap by 20 mm × 30 mm. Each specimen uses glue, cold fabric tape, or an adult-prepared line of six running stitches across the overlap. Adhesive specimens have cured as their labels require.

SAMPLE TEST: an adult supports one end and attaches a sealed 100 g test load to the other for 10 seconds, with the load just above a tray. No pupil hangs weights or pulls a join towards their face. The same load, time and setup are used for every specimen.
REPEAT 1: glue held; tape opened; stitch held.
REPEAT 2: glue held; tape held; stitch opened.
REPEAT 3: glue held; tape opened; stitch held.

“Held” means the layers stayed joined for the full 10 seconds at this load. “Opened” means the overlap separated before 10 seconds. Record observations rather than making the result fit an expected winner.

For real work: pupils can make a fresh glue and cold-tape sample using adult-prepared strips, then label them and leave them to cure. Inspect adult-prepared samples or use these data. Do not test fresh glue just because lesson time is short.

Fair-test check: keep fabric, strip size, overlap, load, time and handling consistent; change the joining method. Repeat specimens to see whether the result is consistent. A 100 g holding test does not find a join’s maximum strength.
answers: Glue held in 3 of 3 sample tests; tape in 1 of 3; stitch in 2 of 3.
In this supplied test, glue gave the most consistent holding result. This does not prove glue is always strongest or suitable for a heavy bag.
Repeat 1 alone gives glue and stitch a tie. The other repeats add evidence.
Do not compare fresh glue with fully prepared tape/stitch and call that a fair test of the methods.

lessons.title: Design for a user
lessons.big_question: Can someone make the item from my plan?
lessons.objective: Develop a labelled textile-item design that uses property evidence, exact dimensions and an ordered making plan.
success: I can identify the user, purpose and testable checks.
I can label fabric, join, size and decoration with reasons.
I can use a partner’s check to improve my making plan.

vocabulary.meaning: The job and checks that a design must satisfy.
A first version made to explore and test a design.
Extra space reserved for a join or construction step.
A measured length, width or height.

slides.title: Design for a user
body: Plan a small card pocket, with a flat-decoration alternative.
Choose a fictional user or keep your idea impersonal.
slides.prompt: What should the drawing tell the maker?
slides.answer: Purpose, material, join, dimensions, decoration position and ordered steps.
slides.notes: Adapts uploaded Week 6. Supplies the missing design sheet, exact pattern and printed original inspiration. Preserves an accessible decoration alternative.

slides.title: Read the pocket brief
body: The club helper needs a desk pocket for a 60 × 50 mm paper task card.
The folded pocket is about 100 × 70 mm, with two 10 mm side joins.
It must accept the card and keep both joins closed through three gentle cycles.
slides.prompt: Which check is about function rather than appearance?
slides.answer: Card fit and side joins holding through three gentle insert/remove cycles.
slides.notes: Not a load-bearing bag or wallet for valuables. The complete printed brief defines the limited use.

slides.title: Compare two original ideas
body: Signal pocket: a large triangle on the front.
Stripe pocket: two broad drawn stripes.
Both keep the opening and side joins clear.
slides.prompt: What would you change for Rowan, who wants a quiet, simple design?
slides.answer: One broad stripe or another simple agreed symbol, while preserving function.
slides.notes: No internet search needed. Credit a feature taken from the idea card and the learner’s deliberate change.

slides.title: Read the dimensions
body: Blank: 100 mm wide and 170 mm high. Measure from the top short edge.
Fold marks: 30 mm and 100 mm down.
Two 10 mm side joins leave about 80 mm inside width.
slides.prompt: Does a 60 mm-wide card have planned clearance?
slides.answer: Yes: 80−60=20 mm total width clearance before thickness and construction variation; check a real model.
slides.notes: Use the exact pattern and 50 mm print-scale line. Do not silently fit the page or change the dimensions.

slides.title: Model the labelled plan
body: Name the actual sample and the property evidence behind its choice.
Show where each cold join goes and which edge stays open.
Place a symbol on the outside front, away from joins.
slides.prompt: What is missing from “Use felt because it is good”?
slides.answer: A relevant observed property, such as flexible/opaque with an edge that stayed together in the sample check.
slides.notes: Model one side join and one label; leave the learner a decision to make.

slides.title: A plan with a flaw
body: The drawing marks tape across all four edges.
It says “card pocket”, but no edge is left open.
slides.prompt: What must change before making?
slides.answer: Keep the pocket opening clear; place tape only on the two planned side strips.
slides.notes: Use paper folds to make the functional problem visible; no adhesive needs to be opened.

slides.title: Create the design
body: Choose user, fabric/sample or model material, cold join and symbol.
Label dimensions and both folds; add a property reason.
Number the making steps and identify the adult approval check.
slides.prompt: Could your partner locate the two side joins?
slides.answer: Pocket: two 10 × 70 mm strips on the bottom panel. Flat decoration: two 10 × 50 mm strips at the smaller panel’s side edges.
slides.notes: GROW core includes reasons and a sequenced plan; adult reads/scribes without replacing decisions.

slides.title: Peer check: could I make it?
body: Find user/purpose, material, join, size and decoration.
Check the making order for your item: pocket folds and opening, or a flat panel join.
Add one missing detail before saving the plan for Week 7.
slides.prompt: Which change made your plan more usable?
slides.answer: For example: adding fold measurements, marking the opening or naming the approved cold tape.
slides.notes: Use the complete checklist. Store the plan with a prepared blank; collect resources and reset. For the flat-decoration route, check panel centring and side joins rather than folds or an opening.

slides.title: Plan the first safe step
body: Finish: “Before I make, I need to check ___.”
slides.prompt: Does a clear drawing prove the finished join will hold?
slides.answer: No. The actual material, approved adhesive preparation and finished join still need testing.
slides.notes: Record practical design reasoning, not artistic drawing skill or a promised award.

worksheet.title: Design for a user | Design and process record

tasks.heading: 1. My user and brief
tasks.prompt: Choose Alex: spot pocket quickly, or Rowan: quiet simple design. Use the supplied pocket brief or state the flat-decoration alternative.
items: Who is the design for and what is its job?
Name two checks your item must meet.
Which printed idea inspired you, and what did you change?
tasks.answer: Pocket: card fits and joins hold for 3 cycles; clear front symbol. Decoration: panels stay attached after 3 gentle lifts and chosen symbol visible. Accept purpose-based changes.

tasks.heading: 2. Label a workable design
tasks.prompt: Draw, trace, dictate or label the pattern for your chosen item.
items: Name the fabric or model material; add a useful property.
Pocket: blank 100 × 170 mm; folds 30 mm and 100 mm from the top; two 10 × 70 mm side joins; opening stays clear.
Flat decoration: backing 100 × 70 mm; front 60 × 50 mm; centre the front and use two 10 × 50 mm side joins. No folds or opening.
Show the front symbol or stripe, clear of the joins.
tasks.answer: Pocket: bottom panel up, flap down, two side joins and clear opening. Flat decoration: centred 60 × 50 mm front on 100 × 70 mm backing, with two side joins and no folds. Accept labelled drawing, tracing, pointing or dictated evidence.

tasks.heading: 3. Make an ordered plan
tasks.prompt: Number these actions, then name one partner-check improvement.
items: Test the item when its joins are ready: pocket card cycles or gentle decoration lifts.
Check plan, materials and approved tools.
Pocket: practise folds without tape. Decoration: centre the front panel without tape.
Apply the correct side tape, assemble and press as instructed.
Decorate the front and allow required drying/handling time.
tasks.answer: Check; rehearse folds or panel position; join/assemble/press; decorate and wait; test the chosen item. Credit one specific plan improvement.

worksheet.exit_question: Why should a pocket’s opening be marked on its plan?
worksheet.exit_answer: So the maker leaves space for the card instead of joining every edge. The flat decoration does not need an opening.

preparation: Print the exact-size pattern, 50 mm scale check, brief and two original inspiration cards. Check print scale before class.
Provide 100 × 170 mm paper blanks and 60 × 50 mm test cards for dry-fold modelling; no adhesive is required today.
Trial the intended cold fabric tape with the actual fabric before Week 7. Choose paper/card model if tape cannot hold or be handled in the session under its product instructions.
materials: Pattern, ruler, pencils/chalk, large paper, brief/idea/checklist cards, optional approved marker.
Known fabric samples or property descriptions; pre-cut paper blanks and test cards.
For flat-decoration choice: 100 × 70 mm backing and 60 × 50 mm front-panel paper models.

timing.activity: Recall one useful property and introduce user choice.
Read brief and compare original ideas.
Model dimensions, joins and a labelled drawing.
Create a labelled plan and dry-fold paper model.
Peer check, improve and sequence making steps.
Store plans, collect pattern pieces and reset.
Individual first-check exit.

teacher.modelling: Show the blank with the short edge at the top. Measure 30 mm then 100 mm from that same origin, not from the first fold. Trace the two side strips; demonstrate why tape across the opening would defeat the pocket’s job.
misconceptions: A picture without dimensions and join labels may be hard for another maker to follow.
Both folds are measured from the original top, not consecutively.
Decoration must not close the opening or hide a faulty join.
A prototype plan is not evidence that the finished join has passed a test.
teacher.support: Offer the two user cards, a pre-marked pattern and a small property-word bank. Learners may trace, position labels, point, dictate or build a paper model; a partner/adult can read the checklist.
teacher.stretch: Calculate 80 mm internal width and 20 mm card clearance; identify how material thickness might affect fit. Justify one change that improves function without enlarging the blank.
teacher.fallback: All inspiration, dimensions and checks are included in print. Use the paper model only; if ruler access is difficult, offer exact pre-cut shapes and measure together.
teacher.safeguarding: Follow the school practical-work risk assessment and individual access plans. The default lessons use no needles, pins, irons, hot glue, cord loops or loose buttons/beads. Adults control, count and return scissors and any small test equipment; pre-cut pieces are available. Use only school-approved cold adhesives according to the actual product instructions, check skin/material sensitivities privately, and keep glue away from eyes and mouths. Touching fabric, wearing an item or accepting physical guidance is never required. Agree support; use demonstration, pointing, an observer role or a paper/card model. Keep personal identifiers and pupil photos off public website files.
teacher.assessment: Look for user/purpose, testable checks, dimensioned material/join labels, a feasible sequence and a revision based on feedback. Assess design communication rather than drawing neatness; distinguish paper model from fabric construction.

resources.title: Design brief | A small card pocket
resources.instructions: This is a lightweight classroom prototype, not a wallet for valuables or a load-bearing bag. The design can be for a fictional club helper; no personal names or disclosures are needed.
items: USER AND PURPOSE: a club helper needs a small soft pocket to keep one paper task card together on the desk. It will be used with its opening upwards.
CARD: the test card is 60 mm wide × 50 mm high. It should slide in and come out without tearing.
SIZE: use one 100 mm × 170 mm fabric blank. The finished folded pocket is about 100 mm wide × 70 mm high. Two 10 mm-wide side joins leave about 80 mm internal width.

FUNCTION: after the appropriate joining/cure time, insert and remove the test card three times. Both side joins should stay closed. This is a desk-use check, not an upside-down shake or a carrying-strength test.

DESIGN: choose an opaque, flexible sample and a suitable cold join. Add a simple symbol or broad stripe on the front to distinguish the pocket. Do not use personal names, cords, sharp fasteners or loose decorations.
PROCESS: the plan must name fabric, join, dimensions, decoration position and ordered making steps. An adult checks the actual tape or adhesive and material before making.
PAPER/CARD ALTERNATIVE: use the same-size paper or light-card blank and school-approved cold tape. Record it as a model of the design, not a fabric-strength result.
answers: The design is judged against purpose, card fit, side-join function and completeness of the plan. Colour preference alone cannot establish those checks.
A 60 mm-wide card fits the planned 80 mm internal width with 20 mm overall clearance, before material thickness and construction variation; test the real model.
No load-bearing or waterproof claim is made.

resources.title: Pattern and fold guide | Exact dimensions
resources.instructions: Use the supplied full-size pattern at 100% or draw it with a ruler. Check the 50 mm scale line before cutting. Do not use “fit to page”. A teacher can trace or pre-cut the blank.
items: Blank: a rectangle 100 mm wide × 170 mm high. Keep the short edge at the top. Use millimetres; 100 mm = 10 cm and 170 mm = 17 cm.

Measure down from the top short edge. Mark a light horizontal fold line at 30 mm. Mark a second fold line at 100 mm. The top 30 mm is the flap; the middle 70 mm is the back; the bottom 70 mm becomes the front.

On the bottom/front panel, mark a 10 mm-wide joining strip at each side: left strip from x = 0 to 10 mm; right strip from x = 90 to 100 mm. Both run from y = 100 to 170 mm. Leave the middle of this panel free of adhesive.

For assembly, fold the bottom 70 mm panel upwards along the 100 mm line, matching its side edges to the middle/back panel. Press only the two side joining strips as the product instructions require. The top edge of the pocket must remain open.
Fold the top 30 mm flap down along the 30 mm line. The flap rests over the opening; it does not need a fastener. The closed outline is approximately 100 mm × 70 mm.
Test card: cut a separate rectangle 60 mm × 50 mm. Use paper or light card, with no confidential details. Slide it through the opening upwards and remove it gently.

Decoration zone: on the outside front after folding, draw one large symbol within an imaginary central 50 mm-wide × 35 mm-high area. Keep decoration away from side joins and the opening. Use a school-approved fabric marker; no added beads/buttons.
This pattern uses two side-join allowances of 10 mm. It is not a stitched seam pattern and should not be resized silently; a size change needs a fresh fit check.
answers: Top-origin fold coordinates: y = 30 mm and y = 100 mm; bottom panel height = 70 mm.
Internal width estimate: 100 − 10 − 10 = 80 mm.
Front panel folds upwards; the top flap folds down. Closing all four edges would trap the card.

resources.title: Two original design ideas | Compare and change
resources.instructions: These written idea cards replace an internet image search. Both use the supplied 100 mm × 170 mm blank. Borrow a design feature and change it for the stated user.
items: IDEA A — Signal pocket: opaque felt; two cold fabric-tape side joins; finished size about 100 mm × 70 mm. A large outlined triangle on the front helps the club helper identify it quickly.
IDEA B — Stripe pocket: the same pocket shape and side joins. Two broad drawn stripes make it look different from other pockets. The flap and opening stay clear.
USER CARD 1 — Alex, a fictional club helper, needs to spot the task-card pocket quickly on a busy desk. A large clear symbol matters more than tiny decoration.
USER CARD 2 — Rowan, a fictional display helper, wants a quiet, simple design. One broad stripe is preferred, and the pocket must still accept the 60 mm × 50 mm card.
Design choices: choose one user, one specimen (or paper model), a tested cold join and a simple front symbol. Explain which feature came from an idea card and what you changed.

If a flat decoration is chosen instead of the pocket: use a 100 mm × 70 mm paper/card-backed fabric panel and a 60 mm × 50 mm front panel, joined with two 10 mm × 50 mm cold-tape strips at the front panel’s side edges. It must stay flat on the desk; do not claim it can contain a card.
answers: For Alex, a large symbol gives a specific purpose-based reason. For Rowan, a broad stripe can satisfy the stated preference.
Many colour and symbol choices are valid; assess labels, purpose and feasibility, not which design the adult prefers.
A flat decoration has a different function: check both panel joins stay attached after three gentle lifts from the desk. It is a legitimate simpler textile-item alternative, not a failed pocket.

resources.title: Plan-review checklist
resources.instructions: One person explains the plan while the other points to each feature. Ask before altering someone else’s drawing.
items: Can I identify the intended user and the item’s limited purpose?
Can I find the chosen material and a relevant observed property?
Can I find the cold joining method and its positions? A pocket also needs a clear opening.
Can I read the dimensions and follow the pocket folds or flat-panel position?
Can I see the symbol/stripe position, clear of the joins and any pocket opening?
Can I follow the making order and locate adult approval plus required handling/cure time?
Can I find the test that will show whether the design meets its brief?
answers: Missing details should lead to one clear revision, such as adding 30/100 mm fold marks or specifying the two side strips.
A valid plan for the flat decoration must use its different two-panel dimensions and attachment test rather than the pocket-card test.

lessons.title: Make, test and improve
lessons.big_question: Does my textile item meet its brief?
lessons.objective: Follow the plan to assemble a prototype, evaluate its function using evidence and make a targeted improvement.
success: I can use my plan and an agreed making sequence safely.
I can record a real test or accurately label a sample-data judgement.
I can explain one improvement linked to an unmet check.

vocabulary.meaning: One check in the design brief.
Judge how well the item meets its stated checks.
Repeat a check after making a change.

slides.title: Make, test and improve
body: Bring back your Week 6 plan. Build the pocket or agreed flat decoration.
Record what you actually make, inspect or model.
slides.prompt: Which two checks matter most for the pocket?
slides.answer: The 60 × 50 mm card fits and both side joins hold through three gentle cycles.
slides.notes: Newly authored Week 7 completion from GROW Autumn SOW row 165: make/evaluate a textile item. No uploaded Week 7 textile deck was supplied; uploaded Week 5–Week 6 provide the precursor work.

slides.title: Check before making
body: Adult confirms the actual material, cold tape and tool arrangements.
Check your prepared blank and fold marks against the pattern.
Know the tape’s required pressing and handling/cure time.
slides.prompt: What if the adhesive cannot be tested before the lesson ends?
slides.answer: Record not yet tested, let it cure and use the supplied fictional record or ready paper model for evaluation.
slides.notes: Never shorten manufacturer preparation/cure requirements to fit the timetable.

slides.title: Dry-fold first
body: Short edge at the top. Bottom panel folds up at 100 mm.
Top 30 mm flap folds down. Reopen the blank before adding side tape.
Check the test card has space; keep the opening clear.
slides.prompt: Where do the two tape strips go?
slides.answer: Along the bottom panel’s outer 10 mm side strips, from 100 mm down to 170 mm.
slides.notes: Model exact fold direction with paper; an adult can position the material if agreed. This slide models the pocket. Flat-decoration makers centre the smaller panel instead of folding; use the alternative construction card.

slides.title: Construct from your plan
body: Pocket: join the two side strips, fold up and press as directed.
Decoration: centre the small panel and join its two side strips; no folding is needed.
Add the planned symbol after checking preparation and handling times.
slides.prompt: What can the checker confirm before the join is fixed?
slides.answer: The side joins and edge or panel alignment match the chosen pattern. A pocket’s opening remains clear.
slides.notes: Use the complete construction card. For the decoration route, follow its two-panel construction instead.

slides.title: A controlled function check
body: When ready: pocket—insert and remove the card three times; decoration—lift gently from the desk three times.
Check both side joins after each cycle and record what happened.
Keep a pocket’s opening upwards. Do not shake, swing or overload either item.
slides.prompt: What result would show the side-join check is met?
slides.answer: Both joins remain attached through all three gentle checks for the chosen item. These results apply only to this limited classroom task.
slides.notes: The test is limited to the card-pocket purpose. Flat decoration uses three gentle lifts from the desk, checking both panel joins.

slides.title: Read a prototype record
body: Sample Pocket B: correct size; card fits at first; left join opens on cycle 2.
The front stripe is clear and the approved preparation was completed.
slides.prompt: Which criterion is not yet met?
slides.answer: The side join staying closed through three cycles. The record supports the other stated checks.
slides.notes: Use the full fictional records if live handling is not possible; do not pass sample results off as a pupil’s practical evidence.

slides.title: Improve one useful thing
body: Name the specific issue and ask before repairing a join.
Change one thing that addresses that issue.
Repeat the relevant check when the repair is ready to handle.
slides.prompt: Would adding a larger symbol repair an opening side join?
slides.answer: No. Repair or redesign the join under adult direction, then retest it.
slides.notes: Keep repairs within the approved method. If time/cure is insufficient, record the next step accurately.

slides.title: Give the evidence-based verdict
body: Use met, not yet or need evidence for each brief check.
Say what you made and the support you used.
Store the item safely; return tools, collect scraps and reset.
slides.prompt: What can you truthfully record if you only made the paper model?
slides.answer: A paper construction/fit model was made; fabric-join performance still needs evidence.
slides.notes: Assess practical process, reasoning and improvement. No personal-disclosure, touch or artistic-neatness requirement.

slides.title: Show the design cycle
body: Finish: “I checked ___; the evidence was ___; next I will ___.”
slides.prompt: Does a neat photograph prove every check passed?
slides.answer: No. It cannot establish test cycles, cure time or the original material/tool approval.
slides.notes: Record individual response using speech, pointing, drawing or scribing.

worksheet.title: Make, test and improve | Design and process record

tasks.heading: 1. My construction record
tasks.prompt: Use your real work or clearly label “paper model” or “fictional record”.
items: I made / modelled / inspected…
One planned dimension or fold I checked was…
One safe making action and the support used were…
tasks.answer: Accept factual observations such as 100 × 170 mm blank, folds at 30/100 mm, clear opening or approved tool check. Do not credit unseen practical work.

tasks.heading: 2. Test against the brief
tasks.prompt: Use your results, or Sample B: pocket 100 × 70 mm, card fits, left join opens on cycle 2, stripe clear. A decoration instead needs centred panels and 3 gentle lift checks.
items: Size and pocket card fit / decoration panel position: met / not yet / need evidence, because…
Both joins through 3 checks: met / not yet / need evidence, because…
Clear front symbol: met / not yet / need evidence, because…
tasks.answer: Sample B: size/initial card fit met; three-cycle join condition not yet; symbol met. For a real decoration, judge actual dimensions/panel centring, both joins after three gentle lifts and the symbol. Record the route and evidence used.

tasks.heading: 3. Improve and retest
items: My issue or missing check is…
One change I would make is…
I would retest by…
If the repair needs more cure time, I will…
tasks.answer: Example: left join opens; adult-guided replacement; repeat 3 gentle card cycles when ready. If curing incomplete, store flat and record not yet tested rather than rushing.

worksheet.exit_answer: A specific change linked to the brief or evidence, followed by the relevant recheck when safe.

preparation: Retrieve Week 6 plans. Prepare/pre-cut 100 × 170 mm blanks, two 10 × 70 mm tape strips and 60 × 50 mm paper test cards; premark folds where useful.
Trial the actual cold tape/material combination and follow its pressing/handling/cure instructions. If readiness extends beyond class, plan the evaluation using a cured model or fictional records.
Prepare a paper model for every pupil who prefers it. Ensure the flat-decoration alternative has 100 × 70 mm backing, 60 × 50 mm front and two 10 × 50 mm joining strips.
materials: Prepared fabric/felt or paper blanks, appropriate school-approved cold tape, ruler, pencil/chalk, approved marker and paper test card.
Week 6 plan, exact pattern, construction card, brief and fictional prototype records.
Adult-controlled counted scissors if needed, table protection, waste tray and flat storage space.

timing.activity: Retrieve plan and choose role/material route.
Adult approval and model folds/joins.
Construct planned prototype or paper model.
Record function evidence and targeted improvement/retest or sample verdict.
Count and return scissors, tools and sample pieces; close approved adhesive containers, collect tape backings and scraps, wipe the work surface as directed and wash hands if needed.
Individual design-cycle exit.

teacher.modelling: Dry-fold a paper blank; show the open top and two side-strip positions. Model one gentle test cycle and a truthful “not yet” record if a join opens. Explain that a repair requires the product’s proper preparation before retesting.
misconceptions: A tidy appearance does not prove function.
Opening on cycle 2 does not meet a 3-cycle holding check.
Decorating cannot fix a structural join.
A model or sample-data judgement must not be recorded as tested fabric construction.
teacher.support: Offer premade fold marks, pre-cut strips and one visible construction step at a time. Learners may direct a maker, point to a check or use paper. Adult support is agreed; no forced physical guidance.
teacher.stretch: Separate size, initial fit and repeated-join evidence; justify a targeted change and identify what an additional long-term test would need to investigate without claiming it has been done.
teacher.fallback: Build the exact paper model or evaluate all three supplied prototype records. A learner can meet the evaluation objective without handling fabric or adhesive; label the route used.
teacher.safeguarding: Follow the school practical-work risk assessment and individual access plans. The default lessons use no needles, pins, irons, hot glue, cord loops or loose buttons/beads. Adults control, count and return scissors and any small test equipment; pre-cut pieces are available. Use only school-approved cold adhesives according to the actual product instructions, check skin/material sensitivities privately, and keep glue away from eyes and mouths. Touching fabric, wearing an item or accepting physical guidance is never required. Agree support; use demonstration, pointing, an observer role or a paper/card model. Keep personal identifiers and pupil photos off public website files.
teacher.assessment: Observe plan use, an agreed safe action, accurate evidence recording and a targeted improvement. Mark met/not yet/need evidence against the selected pocket or decoration brief; do not infer practical competence from a finished photo alone.

resources.title: Make the pocket | Complete construction card
resources.instructions: Allow approximately 17 minutes for assembly using a prepared blank. An adult trials the chosen cold tape on the actual fabric before the lesson and checks its handling/cure instructions. If it cannot be tested within the session, use a pre-cured example or the paper model for evaluation.
items: YOU NEED: one 100 mm × 170 mm approved felt/fabric blank; two 10 mm × 70 mm strips of school-approved cold, pressure-applied fabric tape; a 60 mm × 50 mm paper test card; ruler; pencil/chalk; approved fabric marker. Adult-controlled scissors are optional because all parts can be pre-cut.
1. Read the design brief and your plan. Ask the adult to confirm the material, join and tools are approved. Choose maker, reader or checker roles.
2. Check the blank is 100 mm × 170 mm. With its short edge at the top, mark folds 30 mm and 100 mm down from that edge, or use the pre-marked blank.
3. Practise the folds before adding tape: bottom panel up, top flap down. Check the card can sit inside. Unfold so the joining side faces upwards.

4. Place the two 10 mm × 70 mm cold-tape strips on the left and right edges of the bottom panel only. They run from the 100 mm fold to the bottom edge. Ask the checker to confirm the centre and opening are clear.

5. Remove tape backing as directed, fold the bottom panel up along the 100 mm line and align side edges. Press the two side joins for the time and pressure stated on the product label. Keep the opening clear.
6. Fold the top flap down. Add the planned large symbol or stripe to the outside front using the approved marker. Avoid wet joins and allow any marker drying time required.

7. When the join is ready to handle according to its label, open the flap and gently insert/remove the 60 mm × 50 mm paper card three times. Check fit and both side joins. Record not yet tested if the join needs more cure time.
8. Improve one point if it can be done safely: align an open edge, replace a failed join under adult direction, or clarify the symbol. Repeat the relevant check; do not hide a fault with decoration.
9. Record one observed action and one test result. Store the item flat in the agreed place. Collect tape backings and offcuts; return counted tools and clear the workspace.
PAPER MODEL: use the same blank, folds and test card with suitable cold paper tape. Record a construction/fit model. Its result does not establish that a chosen fabric join will work.

FLAT-DECORATION ALTERNATIVE: use a 100 mm × 70 mm backing and a 60 mm × 50 mm front panel. Centre the smaller panel with 20 mm side margins and 10 mm top/bottom margins. Join its two sides using 10 mm × 50 mm cold-tape strips. Draw a symbol; after the required handling time, lift from the desk three times and check both panel joins remain attached.
answers: Correct pocket folds: bottom up at 100 mm; flap down at 30 mm from the original top. Side tape belongs only on the bottom panel’s two outer 10 mm strips.
Expected pocket checks: test card slides in/out; both joins remain attached for three gentle cycles; planned symbol is visible; opening stays clear. Actual results may differ and must be recorded.
A not-yet-tested record is correct when adhesive or marker needs longer to cure; the pupil can evaluate the provided sample record meanwhile.
Flat decoration: finished backing 100 mm × 70 mm; centred front 60 mm × 50 mm; no card-containment claim.

resources.title: Prototype records | Fictional results
resources.instructions: Use these complete paper records when practical testing is unavailable. They are invented examples, not evidence that a pupil made or tested an item.
items: BRIEF: pocket approximately 100 mm × 70 mm when folded; test card 60 mm × 50 mm fits; both side joins stay closed through three gentle insert/remove cycles; a clear front symbol; adult-approved materials and method.
POCKET A: finished 100 mm × 70 mm; card fits; joins held through all three cycles; a large triangle is visible; the adult-approved tape’s required handling time was completed.
POCKET B: finished 100 mm × 70 mm; card fits at first, but the left join opens on cycle 2. A clear stripe is visible; tape had been correctly prepared and its handling time completed.

POCKET C: finished 100 mm × 70 mm; looks neatly folded, but no card test has happened because the join needs longer to cure. Material and tool checks are recorded; a symbol is planned but not added yet.
Possible verdicts: met = evidence shows the criterion worked; not yet = evidence shows it did not work; need evidence = the check has not happened or its result is missing.
Useful improvement statement: “The left join opened on cycle 2, so I will ask the adult to help replace the join, then repeat three gentle card cycles.”
answers: A: all stated checks are supported by the fictional record.
B: size, initial card fit, visible stripe and approved process are supported; the side-join requirement is not yet met. Repair/retest the join.
C: dimensions and approval are recorded, but card fit and join function need evidence; the symbol is not yet added. Do not test before the join is ready.
A tidy photograph cannot prove a join test or the original material/tool approval.

template_spec.title: Textiles | Full-size pocket and flat-decoration patterns
template_spec.print_instruction: Print at 100% actual size with no fit-to-page scaling. Check the 50 mm calibration line with a ruler before tracing or cutting.
template_spec.coordinate_system: Pattern measurements use a top-left origin: x across to the right, y down. Put all dimension lines outside the cut outline. Native vector drawing only; no raster/image generation or ASCII diagram.

pages.name: Pocket blank
instructions: Cut one 100 × 170 mm blank. Adult may pre-cut and premark.
Dashed lines are folds, not cuts. Two shaded strips show the cold joining zones.
Fold the bottom panel up at 100 mm; fold the flap down at 30 mm. Keep the pocket opening clear.
Closed finished outline is approximately 100 × 70 mm. Pattern includes 10 mm side-join allowances.

pages.name: Test card and optional decoration pieces
instructions: For pocket: use only the 60 × 50 mm paper test card.
For flat decoration: centre the 60 × 50 mm front on the 100 × 70 mm backing; 20 mm side margins and 10 mm top/bottom margins.
Use two 10 × 50 mm approved cold-tape strips at the small front panel’s sides. It is a flat decoration, not a pocket.
Draw a large symbol with an approved marker; do not add cords, sharp fasteners or loose buttons/beads.
